title: Medication Routes and Prescription Terminology

sections.learningObjectives:
- Identify common medication routes of administration and describe how each delivers medication to the body.
- Recognize common prescription terminology, abbreviations, and sig (directions) used in medication orders.
- Explain the importance of clarity in medication orders and apply safe practices for flagging and clarifying unclear orders.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Oral is a fancy word for 'by mouth.' A pill you swallow travels down your food pipe and through your stomach before the medicine gets into your blood, like a letter taking the long road through the mail system.

### Question 2

Sublingual means 'under the tongue.' Think of a sugar cube that melts and soaks in right where you put it, under your tongue.

### Question 3

Topical means 'on the surface,' like sunscreen or lotion you rub on your skin. The medicine works right where you put it.

### Question 4

Ophthalmic is the doctor word for 'eye.' Eye drops go into the eye, so they are ophthalmic, just like glasses are sometimes called 'ophthalmic' lenses.

### Question 5

Otic is the doctor word for 'ear.' If a medicine goes in your ear, it is an otic medicine, like how 'audiology' is the study of hearing.

### Question 6

Inhalation means breathing the medicine in, like breathing in steam from a hot shower. The medicine goes straight down into your lungs with each breath.

### Question 7

Rectal means the medicine goes into the rectum, the last part of the digestive tube. The lining there soaks up medicine a lot like the inside of your mouth soaks up a lozenge.

### Question 8

Intramuscular means 'inside the muscle.' Muscles have lots of blood flowing through them, so medicine injected there gets picked up and carried around the body.

### Question 9

Subcutaneous means 'under the skin,' into the soft fatty layer. It is like tucking the medicine into the padding just below your skin, where it soaks in slowly.

### Question 10

Intravenous means 'inside the vein.' Veins are the highways that carry blood, so medicine put straight into a vein gets to work right away.

### Question 11

Intradermal means 'inside the skin.' It is the most shallow injection of all, like placing a tiny drop just beneath the very top surface of the skin.

### Question 12

Buccal means 'in the cheek.' The medicine sits like a lozenge tucked between your cheek and gum until it melts in.

### Question 13

Nasal just means 'in the nose.' A nasal spray squirts medicine into your nose, like a mist you sniff in.

### Question 14

Vaginal means the medicine is placed inside the vagina, a route used for some creams, tablets, and rings for women's health.

### Question 15

Transdermal means 'through the skin.' A patch is like a slow-drip water bottle taped to your skin, giving a little medicine all day long instead of one big gulp.

### Question 16

Enteral comes from a word meaning 'intestine.' Enteral medicines go through the digestive tube — the mouth, stomach, and gut — like food does.

### Question 17

Parenteral means 'around the intestine,' or skipping the gut. An IV skips the stomach entirely and drops the medicine right into the blood, like a shortcut.

### Question 18

IV medicine is like handing a note straight to the teacher, while a pill is like putting the note in a mailbox and waiting for it to be delivered.

### Question 19

Imagine a toll booth on the road from your stomach to your blood. The liver is that toll booth and it 'charges' by removing some medicine before the rest can reach your body.

### Question 20

Under your tongue is like a fast lane with a direct on-ramp to the bloodstream. A swallowed pill has to go the long way, and the liver takes a toll along that road.

### Question 21

A cream is like sunscreen — it works right on the spot you put it. A patch is like a time-release sponge that soaks medicine through your skin and into your whole body.

### Question 22

A local effect is like putting ice on a sore knee — it only helps the knee. A systemic effect is like drinking a medicine that works all over your body.

### Question 23

If you have a stain on one spot of a shirt, you spot-clean just that spot instead of washing the whole shirt — a topical cream does the same for a rash.

### Question 24

You wouldn't put medicine for your eye inside your ear — the medicine has to go exactly where the problem is, like a repairman going to the right room of the house.

### Question 25

Ear medicine goes in the ear, eye medicine goes in the eye — each medicine has its own doorway, just like each room in a house has its own key.

### Question 26

A vein is a rushing river, so medicine dropped in goes fast. The fat under your skin is more like a slow-draining sponge, so medicine there seeps out gradually.

### Question 27

Asthma medicine is breathed in so it can go straight to the lungs, like sending a fire truck straight to the fire instead of stopping across town first.

### Question 28

If a person can't keep food or pills in their stomach, the medicine can still enter through another doorway, like using the back entrance when the front door is blocked.

### Question 29

Sublingual is like parking under the tongue, and buccal is like parking in your cheek — both are in the mouth, but in different spots.

### Question 30

If a medicine is too big to swallow, the assistant is like a helper who tells the grown-up in charge rather than trying to fix it alone — the doctor or pharmacist picks the right new form.

### Question 31

BID means twice a day — like taking your medicine in the morning and again at night, two times total.

### Question 32

TID means three times a day — like morning, midday, and evening, three doses in one day.

### Question 33

QID means four times a day — think of 'quad,' like four corners of a day.

### Question 34

q4h means every four hours — like setting an alarm to ring again four hours after the last one.

### Question 35

q8h means every eight hours — like clocking in every eight hours around the clock, three times in one day.

### Question 36

AC means before meals — like taking a medicine on an empty stomach before you sit down to eat.

### Question 37

PC means after meals — like taking your medicine right after you finish eating.

### Question 38

HS means at bedtime — think of it as 'hour of sleep,' when you get ready to go to bed.

### Question 39

STAT means 'right now, no waiting' — like a fire alarm that means go immediately.

### Question 40

PRN means 'take it only when you need it' — like reaching for pain medicine only when your head actually hurts, not on a fixed clock.

### Question 41

NPO means 'nothing by mouth' — like a sign on a door that says no food or drink allowed before the test.

### Question 42

The sig is the 'how to take it' part of a prescription — like the instruction line in a recipe that tells you exactly what to do.

### Question 43

Disp means 'dispense' — how much medicine the pharmacist should hand over, like the amount on a grocery order.

### Question 44

Gtt means drops — like counting raindrops, but for eye medicine: two drops in each eye, twice a day.

### Question 45

PR means 'through the rectum' — the medicine goes in through the back passage, like a different doorway the body offers.

### Question 46

tsp is a teaspoon — the small spoon you'd stir tea with, used to measure liquid medicine.

### Question 47

A cap is a capsule — the little medicine container with two halves that fit together. A tab is a tablet — the flat, solid pill.

### Question 48

A suspension is like orange juice with pulp — the bits sink to the bottom, so you shake it to mix it all back in before pouring.

### Question 49

Milliliters measure how much liquid there is, like ounces in a cup. Milligrams measure how heavy a medicine is, like grams on a food scale.

### Question 50

DAW means 'give it exactly as the doctor wrote it, no swaps' — like insisting on the exact brand of snack, not a store-brand lookalike.

### Question 51

Refills are like refill tickets at a drink stand — each one lets you get the medicine again without asking the doctor for a whole new order.

### Question 52

A generic is like the store-brand cereal with the exact same recipe as the name brand — same medicine inside, different label.

### Question 53

The NDC is like a barcode ID for medicine — each exact product and package has its own special number so everyone knows exactly which medicine it is.

### Question 54

DailyMed is like the official instruction booklet for every medicine — it tells exactly what the medicine is for, how it is taken, and what to watch out for.

### Question 55

E-prescribing is like typing and sending an email instead of mailing a messy handwritten note — the computer makes it clear and can even flag mistakes before they happen.

### Question 56

A scheduled medicine is like brushing your teeth at the same times every day. A PRN medicine is like putting a bandage on only when you get a cut.

### Question 57

STAT is like a 'rush' sticker on a package — it means handle it now, not put it in the slow pile.

### Question 58

A complete medicine order is like a complete mailing address — you need the name, the amount, the route (like the street), and how often (like the schedule) for it to get there safely.

### Question 59

If a recipe said 'add flour' but not how much, you wouldn't guess. A medicine order without a route is the same — you ask the person who wrote it.

### Question 60

When the directions say 'by mouth,' that means you swallow it — the mouth is the doorway the medicine uses to get in.

### Question 61

Frequency is how many times a day — 'twice daily' means two times, like a dog that gets walked twice every day.

### Question 62

'Take with food' is like eating a little something first so the medicine sits more gently in your tummy, like putting padding before a load.

### Question 63

When the directions say 'apply,' it usually means rub it on the skin, like putting lotion on dry hands.

### Question 64

Saying 'each eye' in full words is like writing a name on a lunchbox in big clear letters so nobody grabs the wrong one.

### Question 65

Under the tongue is the 'sublingual' spot — like letting a mint melt under your tongue instead of chewing and swallowing it.

### Question 66

'Take as directed' is like a treasure map that says 'go somewhere' without telling you where or how far — not enough information to follow safely.

### Question 67

If you can't read a note, you don't guess what it says — you ask the person who wrote it. Guessing with medicine could really hurt someone.

### Question 68

ISMP is like a safety coach for medicine — it studies mistakes and publishes rules so doctors, nurses, and pharmacists avoid making them.

### Question 69

A fuzzy medicine order is like a fuzzy stop sign — if someone misreads it, something bad can happen. Clear writing keeps everyone safe.

### Question 70

Two medicine names that look or sound almost the same are like two classmates named 'Sarah' and 'Sara' — easy to mix up, and mixing up medicine is dangerous.

### Question 71

Tall man lettering makes the important, different letters stand up tall so your eye catches them — like putting a big red underline on the one letter that matters.

### Question 72

Medication reconciliation is like checking your suitcase against the packing list before a trip to make sure nothing is missing or doubled up.

### Question 73

A patch is like a slow, steady drip instead of a big splash — it keeps the medicine level even all day and night.

### Question 74

An IV is the express lane straight into the blood, while a pill, a cream, and a patch all have to wait in line to be absorbed.

### Question 75

Absorption is the waiting game of getting medicine from outside into the blood. An IV skips the game by starting inside the blood already.

### Question 76

The route is the road the medicine takes. A highway gets there fast, a dirt road slow — the medicine is the same, but the trip is different.

### Question 77

Breathing asthma medicine sends it straight to the lungs, like watering just the one thirsty plant instead of hosing down the whole garden.

### Question 78

Writing down the route is like writing down the road you drove on — it tells the next person exactly how the medicine got where it was going.

### Question 79

No refills left means the 'refill tickets' are all used up, so the doctor has to write a fresh one — the assistant's job is to help get that new order.

### Question 80

q6h means every six hours — like setting an alarm that goes off again six hours after each dose.

### Question 81

'On an empty stomach' means take it when your tummy is empty, like before breakfast — so the medicine doesn't have to share space with food.

### Question 82

If someone keeps needing the 'as needed' medicine all the time, that's a clue to tell the doctor — like noticing a leaky faucet and calling the plumber instead of ignoring it.

### Question 83

If someone is asleep and can't swallow, you can't give them a pill — the medicine has to go in a different way, like through a vein, decided by the doctor.

### Question 84

The doctor is like the chef who picks whether the medicine comes as a pill, a liquid, or a patch — the assistant helps by sharing helpful information, not by deciding.

### Question 85

The route is the 'where and how' of the medicine — like telling a delivery driver whether to use the front door, the back door, or the garage. It changes everything.
